newsitem.title: ITALY: ATHLETICS-IAAF ACCEPT NATIONAL TWO-YEAR BAN LIMITS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-IAAF ACCEPT NATIONAL TWO-YEAR BAN LIMITS.

text.p: The world governing body of athletics said on Friday it would not challenge two-year bans handed to athletes from countries whose national laws do not allow more severe sanctions for doping offences.

The International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) Council said athletes from countries who only permit two-year bans, will be reinstated for competition after that period under the IAAF's "exceptional circumstances" rule.
The IAAF's policy of banning doping offenders for four years will be reviewed at the full IAAF Congress in Athens during late July.
Germany, Russia and Spain permit only two-year bans.
"It is unfair and we recognise the division but there is little we can do about it until the situation is re-examined by the IAAF Congress," said Ana Legnani, an IAAF spokeswoman.
The IAAF Doping Commission believes a two-year ban should be imposed, but a move to reduce the term was defeated by the IAAF Congress two years ago in Gothenburg.

The case of four Greek athletes, including world indoor 60 metres champion Haralambros Papadias, who are alleged to have avoided out-of-competition testing while training in Germany on March 6, has been referred back to the Greek athletics federation.
The Greek federation has been told to report back to the IAAF Doping Commission with a full report within three weeks.
British shot putter Paul Edwards, who was sent home from the 1994 Commonwealth Games after providing two positive tests, has had his appeal for early reinstatement rejected by the IAAF Council.
